title: Refeeds and diet breaks during a cut
chunks: Long diets are physically and mentally taxing. Refeeds and diet breaks are planned, structured increases in calories that can make a cut more sustainable. They are tools for adherence and recovery, not cheat days or excuses to binge.

A refeed is a short rise in calories — usually one to two days — mostly from carbohydrates, bringing you up to roughly maintenance. It refills muscle glycogen, can support training performance, and gives a psychological breather. Keep protein steady and add the extra calories mainly through carbs.

A diet break is a longer pause — typically one to two weeks at maintenance calories — taken after several weeks of dieting. It can reduce diet fatigue, restore some hormones affected by prolonged restriction, and renew motivation before you resume the deficit.

Expect the scale to jump up during a refeed or diet break. This is glycogen and the water stored with it (about 3 g of water per gram of glycogen), not fat. The weight comes back off within days of returning to your deficit.

A common structure is to diet for 6–12 weeks, then take a 1–2 week diet break at maintenance, repeating as needed. Leaner individuals and longer cuts benefit most. If you are only a few weeks into a cut and feeling fine, you probably do not need one yet.
Refeeds and breaks are most useful when diet fatigue, poor sleep, low energy, stalled progress, or strong cravings start to build. Used well, they help you finish a cut rather than abandoning it.

These tools assume a healthy relationship with food. If structured calorie increases trigger guilt, loss of control, or compensatory behavior, that is a sign to step back and speak with a doctor or registered dietitian rather than pushing through.
